items.title: The Phases of Transcription and mRNA Processing

source_refs.note: The phases of transcription with both For Information boxes and post-transcriptional modifications (PDF 133-136); Figures 19.13 to 19.16 are replaced by original diagrams.

blocks.text: No primer is needed. RNA polymerase binds the template DNA at a special nucleotide sequence, the promoter, which is not itself transcribed.

blocks.caption: Promoter sequences
rows: -35 sequence, about 35 nucleotides before the start point

blocks.alt: Two DNA lines with promoter boxes before a +1 start arrow. Prokaryote: TTGACA labelled -35 sequence and TATAAT labelled -10 sequence. Eukaryote: GGCCAATCT labelled CAAT box (-70) and TATAAA labelled TATA box (-25). Below: the five subunits of prokaryotic RNA polymerase, two alpha, beta prime, beta and sigma, with their roles.
blocks.caption: Promoters and the subunits of RNA polymerase (original diagram after Figure 19.13).
blocks.long_description: Transcription needs no primer. RNA polymerase binds a special sequence, the promoter, which is not itself transcribed. In prokaryotes the promoter has TTGACA about 35 nucleotides before the start point (the -35 sequence) and TATAAT about 10 before it (the -10 sequence); in eukaryotes the TATA box TATAAA lies about 25 before (-25) and the CAAT box GGCCAATCT about 70 before (-70). Prokaryotic RNA polymerase has five subunits: two alpha subunits bind regulatory proteins, beta prime binds the template DNA, beta binds the RNA nucleotides and sigma recognises the promoter and starts synthesis.

blocks.text: RNA polymerase has five subunits: two alpha subunits bind regulatory proteins, beta prime binds the template DNA, beta binds RNA nucleotides, and sigma recognises the promoter and initiates synthesis. After the enzyme attaches to the promoter the sigma subunit is removed, and the other four, the core enzyme, unwind the helix and break the base pairs, forming the transcription bubble in which the RNA chain is assembled.

blocks.title: For information: RNA polymerases
blocks.text: Prokaryotes have one RNA polymerase, which makes all three kinds of RNA. Eukaryotes have three: RNA polymerase I makes rRNA in the nucleolus, RNA polymerase II makes mRNA and RNA polymerase III makes tRNA.

Inside the bubble RNA polymerase builds a chain of complementary ribonucleotides along the template in the 5' to 3' direction, usually starting with A or G. The nucleotides come as ribonucleoside triphosphates (rNTPs); as each is added two phosphates detach with release of energy. The first 12 bases of the new mRNA, as the book gives it, form a temporary helix with the template that keeps the 3' end in place to receive the next nucleotide; the RNA-DNA helix rotates as each nucleotide is added, keeping the 3' end at the catalytic site. The bubble moves along the DNA, the growing mRNA protrudes from it, and the DNA re-winds behind.

blocks.alt: Top: a transcription bubble where the DNA strands are apart inside a dashed outline of RNA polymerase; red RNA pairs with the template strand for a short stretch, the RNA-DNA helix, and its 5' end trails out of the bubble. Bottom: termination, with the RNA folded into a hairpin held by G-C pairs, followed by UUUU paired weakly with AAAA on the template, the polymerase pausing and the RNA released.
blocks.caption: Elongation in the transcription bubble and termination at a GC hairpin (original diagram after Figures 19.14 and 19.15).
blocks.long_description: After binding the promoter, RNA polymerase loses its sigma subunit; the core enzyme unwinds the DNA to form a transcription bubble. Inside it the enzyme builds RNA complementary to the template strand in the 5' to 3' direction, usually starting with A or G, from ribonucleoside triphosphates, two phosphates being released from each with energy. The first bases of the new RNA form a temporary helix with the template, keeping the 3' end at the active site; the bubble moves along and the DNA re-winds behind it. At the end of the gene a GC-rich region followed by AT pairs is transcribed; the RNA forms a GC hairpin that makes the polymerase pause, and the weak U-A pairs then let the RNA separate, ending transcription.

blocks.text: At the end of a gene there is a stop region: a series of G-C base pairs followed by a series of A-T pairs. When it is transcribed, hydrogen bonds form within the mRNA strand, making a loop called the GC hairpin, followed by a tail of four or more U nucleotides. The hairpin makes RNA polymerase pause, and the U-A pairs between the RNA and the DNA, the weakest pairs, cannot hold the RNA-DNA hybrid together during the long pause, so the RNA separates and transcription stops.
Prokaryotes have no nucleus, so their mRNA, made in the cytoplasm, starts translation at once. In eukaryotes the new mRNA must travel from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, and on the way it is modified.

blocks.alt: Three rows. A new mRNA of exon 1, intron, exon 2, intron, exon 3. The same with an orange cap at the 5' end and a green AAAA...A tail at the 3' end. The mature mRNA with the introns removed and exons 1, 2 and 3 joined between the cap and the tail. A note explains the cap, tail and splicing.
blocks.caption: Cap, tail and splicing of eukaryotic mRNA (original diagram after Figure 19.16).
blocks.long_description: Prokaryotic mRNA is used at once, but eukaryotic mRNA must travel from the nucleus to the cytoplasm and is first modified. A methylated G nucleotide is joined 5' to 5' to the first nucleotide to form the 5' cap, which protects the mRNA from nucleases and phosphatases. About 250 A nucleotides are added at the 3' end as the poly-A tail, which also protects it from breakdown. The new mRNA contains exons, which are translated, and introns, which are not; splicing removes the introns and joins the exons to give the mature mRNA.

items: 5' cap: the first nucleotide of the mRNA is A or G; a methylated G nucleotide is joined to it by a 5' to 5' bond. The cap protects the mRNA from nucleases and phosphatases on its journey.
3' poly-A tail: a chain of about 250 A nucleotides added at the 3' end, which protects the mRNA from breakdown by nucleases.
Splicing: the new mRNA contains introns, which do not code for protein, and exons, which are translated. Splicing removes the introns and joins the exons to give mature mRNA.

blocks.prompt: Why does eukaryotic mRNA need a cap and a tail but prokaryotic mRNA does not?
blocks.explanation: Eukaryotic mRNA must travel from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, and the cap and tail protect it from enzymes on the way. Prokaryotic mRNA is made in the cytoplasm and translated at once.

items: Initiation: RNA polymerase (sigma) binds the promoter; no primer.
Elongation: RNA made 5' to 3' from rNTPs in a moving bubble.
Termination: GC hairpin + U tail releases the RNA.
Eukaryotes: 5' cap, poly-A tail, splicing of introns.
